Point a device at HotLoop's broker and it shows up. Its sensors read, its
switches show their state, its entities have the names, units and classes it
announced. Nobody types a tag list.

And it can't command a damn thing. Every point discovery makes is read-only, and
it stays that way until an admin accepts the device and then arms each point by
hand, looking at the exact topic the command will go to. A device announcing
itself is a device telling you what it is. That's useful. It is not a device
earning the right to flip a relay on your plant, and HotLoop doesn't pretend it
is.

## What speaks it

The format is the one with topics like `homeassistant/sensor/kitchen/power/config`.
It carries the name of the project that defined it; HotLoop speaks it because
the publishers do, and that's the whole relationship.

| Publisher | How it gets here | What we test it against |
|---|---|---|
| **ESPHome** (its `mqtt:` component) | per component, on by default, retained | recorded output of real nodes (see below) |
| **Zigbee2MQTT** | per component, with templates on nearly everything | recorded output of real installs |
| **Tasmota** | its own format, below | recorded output of nine real devices |
| **Shelly** (Gen2, Gen3, Gen4) | no announcement at all; learned from the statuses it publishes, below | recorded output of fifteen sets of real messages and the maker's documentation |
| Anything else that publishes the format | the same | the format's own rules |

About ESPHome: the plan was to run a real ESPHome firmware in CI, built for the
`host` platform. It doesn't work. ESPHome 2026.9.1's `mqtt:` component is only
available on ESP32, ESP8266, BK72xx, LN882x and RTL87xx, and `esphome config` on
a host build says exactly that and stops. So ESPHome is held to recordings of
real nodes, the same as Zigbee2MQTT, which won't start without a Zigbee radio.

The recordings are in `internal/discovery/testdata`. Every file is messages a
real install published, captured by the person running it and posted in a
public issue, headed with the publisher and version, the device, the link, and
exactly what was changed (almost always nothing but JSON whitespace). They are
what CI checks every config, every template and every state payload against.

## Tasmota

Current Tasmota doesn't publish the `homeassistant/` format. Its docs say that
was removed from every build. What it publishes, retained, is its own:

- `tasmota/discovery/<MAC>/config`: the device (its topic, its full-topic
  pattern, its relays and lights, its on and off words, its last-will words);
- `tasmota/discovery/<MAC>/sensors`: what its sensors read right then.

Both are written by `TasDiscovery` in Tasmota's `xdrv_12_discovery.ino` (read at
arendst/Tasmota `development` 5c295fb, 2026-10-12). HotLoop turns the two into
the same components every other publisher makes, so everything after (the
Discovered screen, accepting, arming, the write gate, the reading) is one code
path. The MAC is the device's identity; a device that is also announcing in the
`homeassistant/` format (an old firmware with SetOption19) is the same device.

| Tasmota says | HotLoop makes |
|---|---|
| a relay (`rl` 1) | a switch: reads `stat/<topic>/POWER` (`POWER1`, `POWER2` and so on when there's more than one), in the device's own on and off words; commands `cmnd/<topic>/POWER[n]` with ON or OFF |
| a light (`rl` 2) | a light: on and off the same way. With one dimmer, its level is the `Dimmer` key of `tele/<topic>/STATE`, 0 to 100, and is set with `cmnd/<topic>/Dimmer` |
| every number in the sensors message | a sensor each, read from `tele/<topic>/SENSOR` by its path (`ENERGY` `Power`, `SCD40` `CarbonDioxide`), with the unit and class Tasmota gives that name. A three-phase meter's array is one sensor per phase |
| its last will | availability: `tele/<topic>/LWT`, with the device's own Online and Offline words |

Topics are built the way Tasmota builds them: its full topic with `%prefix%`
and `%topic%` filled in, so a device whose owner changed the full topic
(`tasmota/35D7A0/%prefix%/`, or `bi/test/%topic%/%prefix%`) reads and commands
on the topics it actually uses.

What it doesn't read, it says, in the source's problems and never by silence:
shutters, a switch input, a button, an iFan, a camera, the colors of a color
light, and the brightness of a device with more than one light. Nothing in the
recordings shows any of those working, so nothing here claims to read them.

**Asking.** Tasmota reports a relay when it changes and everything every five
minutes. So when a device starts being read, HotLoop sends one empty message to
`cmnd/<topic>/POWER`, which Tasmota answers with the state of every relay and
moves nothing; without it a device that hasn't changed reads unknown for up to
five minutes after HotLoop starts. The message is empty, to a topic that ends
in `POWER` and nothing else, and a listen-only source sends nothing at all.

**A light's brightness** arrives with Tasmota's telemetry (every five minutes
unless the device's `TelePeriod` is shorter), not the moment it changes. On
and off arrive at once.

**On each broker** the format is a switch (`tasmota` on the broker, in
Settings, MQTT). A broker added now has it on; the embedded broker always has
it; a broker that already existed keeps listening exactly as before, so it's
off until somebody turns it on. Off means HotLoop doesn't even subscribe to
`tasmota/discovery/#` there.

A config is untrusted like any other. One published under a MAC that isn't
the one it says it is, a full topic with no `%topic%` or with a wildcard, a
topic with a slash in it, an on word with a quote in it, a version it doesn't
know: each is refused with why, and nothing is made. A sensor name with a
quote in it never reaches a template.

**What this was tested against.** Nine devices' real messages, captured from
Tasmota's own console and posted in its public issue tracker, in
`internal/discovery/testdata/tasmota`, each headed with the link, the version
and what was changed (nothing but whitespace, and a redacted MAC):

| Recording | Device | Source |
|---|---|---|
| esp32-8relay-13.4.0 | ESP32 board, 8 relays, Tasmota 13.4.0 | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/20953 |
| esp32-zigbee-gateway-reboots-15.3.0.1 | ESP32 with no relays, three boots | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/24487 |
| esp8266-sps30-scd40-airsensor-14.1.0 | CO2 and particulate sensor, 14.1.0 | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/24780 |
| esp8266-sps30-scd40-airsensor-15.4.0-invalid-json | the same box on 15.4.0, whose firmware published JSON with a trailing comma | the same issue |
| nous-a1t-energy-plug-14.5.0 | NOUS A1T plug with energy metering | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/23094 |
| olimex-esp32-poe-counter-custom-fulltopic-14.5.0 | counters and a three-phase meter, full topic changed | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/23775 |
| shelly-dimmer2-15.3.0.3 | Shelly Dimmer 2 running Tasmota | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/24560 |
| tuyamcu-energy-meter-custom-fulltopic-14.5.0 | TuyaMCU energy meter, full topic changed | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/23165 |
| wemos-2relay-15.1.0.1 | two relays, from Tasmota's author's own console log | github.com/arendst/Tasmota/issues/24006 |

These are recordings, not a device on the bench. A Tasmota on the lab bench
isn't here yet, so this is verified against recorded output of real devices
and not against one running now. The things the recordings don't have are the
brightness (the dimmer's own `tele/STATE` line was garbled in its source log;
its `Dimmer` key is in the same recording's `STATUS11`, which Tasmota builds
with the same function) and the power query being answered (the recordings
show the question and the answer, from Tasmota's console, not HotLoop asking).

## Shelly

A Shelly Gen2, Gen3 or Gen4 announces nothing. There is no config topic to wait
for. What it does, once MQTT is on and its status notifications are on, is
publish each component's whole status on `<prefix>/status/<component>`
(`switch:0`, `cover:0`, `light:0`, `input:0`, a virtual `boolean:200`) every time it changes, and its last will on `<prefix>/online`.
So HotLoop learns the device from what it says: the components it has
published, the fields each one has carried, and the MAC from its `sys` status.
The prefix is the device's id by default (`shellyplus2pm-485519968144`), which
is its model and its MAC, so a device on its default prefix doesn't even wait
for `sys`. One on a prefix somebody typed (`ShellyLichtGarten`) has to publish
`sys` before it can be told apart from another one, and until it does it is
named in the source's problems and not made.

What was learned is kept, per prefix, and only ever grows. A component that
goes quiet hasn't been removed, and a status with less in it than the last one
takes nothing away, so a restart doesn't make a device lose parts. Everything
after that is the same path as every other publisher: the Discovered screen,
accepting, arming each point, the write gate, the reading.

| Shelly says | HotLoop makes |
|---|---|
| `switch:n` with an `output` | a switch: reads `output` from `<prefix>/status/switch:n`; commands `<prefix>/command/switch:n` with `on` or `off` |
| `light:n` | a light the same way, with `set,true` and `set,false`; with `brightness` in its status, a level 0 to 100, sent as `set,true,<level>` |
| `cover:n` | a cover: reads `state` (open, closed, opening, closing, stopped) and sends `open`, `close` and `stop`. A cover that says `pos_control` is calibrated, so it also reads `current_pos` and is sent `pos,<n>`; one that isn't only opens and closes |
| `apower`, `voltage`, `current`, `freq`, `pf`, `aenergy.total`, `temperature.tC` on a switch, light or cover | a sensor each, in W, V, A, Hz, Wh and degrees C, with the class Shelly's documentation gives them |
| `input:n` | a binary sensor of its `state` |
| `devicepower:n`, `voltmeter:n`, `illuminance:n`, `presencezone:n` | sensors and binary sensors of battery, external power, voltage, light level, presence and the number of objects |
| `boolean:n`, `number:n`, `enum:n` (virtual components) | read-only sensors. Setting a virtual component is an RPC call, which this doesn't do, and each one is said in the source's problems |
| its `online` last will | availability, with Shelly's own `true` and `false` |

The commands are the ones the maker's MQTT page lists under MQTT Control, and
the tests hold HotLoop to that list: `on`, `off` and `toggle` for a switch;
`set,<bool>,<brightness>` for a light; `open`, `close`, `stop` and `pos,<n>` for
a cover. Every one is a write through the gate, armed by a person.

**Asking.** A Shelly publishes a component when it changes, so a device that
hasn't changed would read unknown until it does. When a device starts being
read, HotLoop sends `status_update` to `<prefix>/command`, which the same page
says makes the device publish its components' status and moves nothing. It is
that one word, to a topic that ends in `/command` and nothing else, and a
listen-only source sends nothing at all. It happens each time the device's
reading starts, so arming several points in a row asks several times.

**What the device has to have on.** MQTT enabled, with the broker's address;
status notifications on (`status_ntf`); and, for commands, control on
(`enable_control`). HotLoop's own broker has a `shelly` login profile, named
after the device's prefix, that lets it publish its statuses and hear
`<prefix>/command` and nothing else.

**What it doesn't read.** Said, in the source's problems, never by silence: a
component of a kind it hasn't been shown (`lora:100` on a Gen4 with the LoRa
add-on, a `pm1`, an `em`), a switch or a cover that has left out the field it is
read from, and a virtual component's setting. Input events (a double push, a
long push) arrive on the RPC notification topic, `<prefix>/events/rpc`, and
aren't read; only an input's `state` is. A prefix with more than two levels
(`home/garage/boiler`) isn't heard; one or two are. Nothing is sent over RPC.

**On each broker** it's a switch (`shelly` on the broker, in Settings, MQTT).
A broker added now has it on; the embedded broker always has it; a broker that
already existed keeps listening exactly as before, so it's off until somebody
turns it on. It is a switch because the topics it listens on, `+/status/+`, are
wide, and a broker that carries something else under `*/status/*` wants it off.
Off means HotLoop doesn't subscribe to them there.

It's untrusted like any other topic. A prefix that isn't letters, digits and
`_.-`, a component that isn't `kind:number`, a payload that isn't an object or
is over 64 KiB, a device that says more than 64 components, and more than 512
devices being learned at once are each ignored, and a structure kept under one
prefix that says it is another is refused.

**What this was tested against.** Fifteen sets of real messages and the maker's
documentation, in `internal/discovery/testdata/shelly`. The device recordings
are mostly the debug logs of the ioBroker Shelly adapter, posted in its public
issue tracker (one comes from another project's), each headed with the link, the device,
the firmware where the post gives one and what was changed (whitespace). The
documentation files are the maker's own examples, fetched on 2026-10-02 and
2026-10-12.

| Recording | Device | Source |
|---|---|---|
| plus-1-fw1.4.2-switch-rpc | Plus 1, firmware 1.4.2 | github.com/iobroker-community-adapters/ioBroker.shelly/issues/1055 |
| plus-2pm-cover-mode | Plus 2PM as a roller shutter, calibrated | the same repository, issues/1088 |
| 1pm-mini-gen3-fw2.0.0-switch | 1PM Mini Gen3, 2.0.0 | the same, issues/1592 |
| 2pm-gen3-fw2.0.1-beta3-switch | 2PM Gen3, 2.0.1-beta3, two channels | the same, issues/1627 |
| 2pm-gen4-lora-addon | 2PM Gen4 with the LoRa add-on | the same, issues/1349 |
| plug-s-gen3-fw2.0.1-beta1-switch | Plug S Gen3 | the same, issues/1594 |
| pro4pm-gen2-fw2.0.1-switch-set | Pro 4PM, 2.0.1, with the poster's MAC redacted | the same, issues/1640 |
| pro-dimmer-2pm-fw1.3.0-light | Pro Dimmer 2PM | the same, issues/974 |
| dimmer-gen3-light-sys | Dimmer Gen3 | github.com/enesbcs/shellyteacher4domo/issues/65 |
| pill-gen3-fw1.8.99 | Pill, 1.8.99, with a voltmeter | the ioBroker repository, issues/1232 |

| frankever-sprinkler-virtual-components | a sprinkler controller on a prefix of its own, virtual components | the same, issues/1207 |
| official-docs-component-status | the maker's component examples: Plus 1PM, Plus 2PM, H&T, Pro 1, WDUS | shelly-api-docs.shelly.cloud |
| official-docs-mqtt-control | the maker's MQTT Control commands | the same |
| official-docs-mqtt-page, official-docs-notifications | the maker's MQTT page and notification examples | the same |

Two of them can't be built into a device, and the tests say so: the Pro 4PM's
prefix has the poster's redaction in it (`xxxx`) and no `sys`, and the garden
light's is a prefix of its own with none either. Both wait for their MAC, as a
real one would.

**This is verified against recordings and the documentation, and not against a
Shelly on the bench.** None is here yet. The statuses are what real devices
published, the topics HotLoop reads are topics those devices used, and the
commands are in the forms the maker documents. What the recordings can't show:
a command actually moving a relay, a cover actually going to a position, and
the `status_update` answer. When a Shelly is on the bench, those are the three
things to try first.

## What happens when something announces itself

1. **It appears.** On the embedded broker, a device that announces itself is a
   HotLoop device straight away: protocol `mqtt`, not placed on the tree, named
   after what it called itself (`kitchen-plug`, then `-2` on a collision),
   reading. Its tags are named after what it announced (`power`, `relay`). Its
   entities get the name, device class, state class, unit, category and icon
   the config gave them, and an entity the config says is off by default starts
   disabled.
2. **Nothing is armed.** Every tag is created read-only. A switch, a number or
   a text gets its control entity at once, unarmed (`armed: false`), so a screen
   or an automation can name `switch.kitchen_plug_relay` from day one. It starts
   working the moment a person arms the point, and not before.
3. **An admin decides.** Devices, Discovered. Who announced it (on the
   embedded broker, the login and client id that published its config), every
   component it would make, every topic it reads, every command topic in full,
   and what to look at:

   - a command topic outside the topics the component reads (a "lamp" whose
     commands go to `cmnd/boiler/POWER`);
   - a command topic inside the discovery prefix, or one another device also
     claims;
   - a config that asks for retained commands, because a retained command
     replays every time the device reconnects;
   - templates HotLoop can't evaluate, and config keys the format doesn't define.

   **Accept** keeps it reading and makes its points armable, one at a time, in
   the tag editor. It arms nothing. If the device suggested an area and a tree
   node has exactly that name, the accept dialog pre-fills it. A publisher
   doesn't get to file itself under Boiler Room; a person clicks accept.
   **Ignore** drops the device, tags and entities (history stays, like any
   device's) and keeps it dropped when it announces again. Deleting a
   discovered device is the same as ignoring it, because one that keeps
   announcing would just come back.

## When it changes its mind

**A different login is held for review, whatever it says.** On the embedded
broker, a device remembers the login it was accepted from. The same device announced by another login is held
for review with the two logins side by side, even when the config is word for
word the same, and the log gets a warning. Either somebody moved the device to
a new login, or a login is announcing a device that isn't its own. Apply, and
the new login is the one it's accepted from. Reject, and that login announcing
the same thing stays rejected.

**A config that changes under an accepted device is held for review.** The
accepted config keeps running. The Discovered screen shows the change field by
field, running against announced, and an admin applies or rejects it. A unit
going from °C to °F, or a state topic pointed somewhere else, is exactly how a
wrong number gets a trusted face. Applying a change never changes whether a
point is armed: that was a person's decision and stays one.

A firmware update, a new device name, a new model or a different icon applies by
itself. Nobody should have to click for a version bump.

Before anybody accepts a device, the newest announcement always applies:
nobody has built on it yet.

**An empty config withdraws a component.** Its points read bad, saying
"withdrawn by the publisher at 14:02", and nothing is deleted. An alarm on that
point keeps its target and says why it's bad. If the same component comes back,
it's reinstated, and until it sends a new value it reads "announced again after
a withdrawal; waiting for its next value" rather than passing off the value from
before it left. A device nobody accepted that withdraws every component it had
is gone, because nobody built on it.

**Zigbee2MQTT renaming a device** clears its old config topics and announces
new ones with the same unique IDs. HotLoop keys components on the unique ID, so
that's a withdrawal and a reinstatement a second apart, and nothing is lost.

## Reading

A state goes through the component's value template, if it has one, and then
through the component's own matching: `payload_on`/`payload_off` for a binary
sensor (`ON`/`OFF` by default), `state_on`/`state_off` for a switch, a number for
a number, one of the options for a select. **Anything that doesn't fit is a bad
reading with the reason**, shown on the tile:

- `"CLOSE" is neither payload_on "CLOSED" nor payload_off "OPEN"`
- `value_json has no key 'temperature'`
- `"unavailable" is not a number`
- `the publisher sent no value` (it sent `None`, `null`, nothing, or `unknown`)
- `no update for 300 s (expire_after)`

The first one is real: Zigbee2MQTT 1.41.0 announces an Avatto TRV07's window
sensor that way, and the person who captured it opened an issue because the
window never showed. HotLoop shows it bad and says why instead of guessing.

**Availability** is the device's link, not a reading. While the device says
it's offline on its availability topic, it shows disconnected with its own
words ("the device says it is offline (plug/status = offline)") and its entities
are unavailable. Until the first availability message arrives, a device with
availability configured isn't available. That's the format's rule, and it's the
right one. The broker session isn't torn down for it: it's shared with every
other device on that broker.

`expire_after` makes a value bad after that many seconds without an update.
`off_delay` turns a binary sensor off after that many seconds, because the
config says the device never sends the off. JSON attributes land on the entity,
up to 64 keys and 8 KiB, under HotLoop's own (`friendly_name`, `source`,
`armed` and the rest always win).

A component with no state topic reads bad forever. HotLoop never assumes a
state from a command.

## Commands

Nothing is commanded until three things are true, in this order:

1. **A person accepted the device.** Until then the tag editor won't arm a
   point on it ("accept the device first"), and the write gate refuses its
   commands on its own, so a hand-edited row or an old backup with the point
   armed gets nowhere either.
2. **A person armed the point**, in the tag editor, one at a time. Before the
   checkbox, the editor says where the commands go and what they send:
   "Commands go to `plug/relay/set`, sending ON or OFF."
3. **The write gate lets the command through**, like every other write: writes
   switched on, the MCP switch for an agent, the tag's range, the entity's own
   checks, a live session. Audited with its call id, refused or not. The dry
   run asks exactly the same questions.

What goes out is what the config says: `payload_on` and `payload_off` for a
switch, `payload_press` for a button, the option for a select, the value for a
number or a text (a whole number as one, `5` not `5.0`), through the config's
command template when it has one. A button presses once. Its "release" would be a
second command the device never asked for, so a discovered button is single
shot.

A light gets `payload_on`/`payload_off` (a JSON-schema light, `{"state":"ON"}`),
and a brightness in percent scaled to its own `brightness_scale` and rounded,
on its brightness command topic (a JSON-schema light, `{"state":"ON",
"brightness":128}`). A cover gets `payload_open`, `payload_close` or
`payload_stop`, and a position scaled from percent into its own
`position_closed`..`position_open` through `set_position_template`. A valve
gets its open and close payloads (a valve that reports a position, its
`position_open` and `position_closed`), a position on its command topic, and
`payload_stop` once: like a button, a discovered valve's stop is single shot.
A payload the config switches off with `null` (a cover with no stop) is a
command the gate refuses with why.

The gate refuses a command, with the reason, when:

- nobody has accepted the device;
- the broker it's on is listen-only;
- the publisher withdrew the component;
- its command template is outside the subset ("command template not
  supported: filter `regex_replace` is not supported at column 12"). It is never
  "send the raw value instead";
- its config has no command topic;
- its config has no payload for what was asked: a stop on a cover whose
  config says `payload_stop: null`, an option a select doesn't have, a
  brightness above 100%. The payload is rendered in the check, so the dry run
  says no too.

**Retained commands follow the config.** If a config asks for `retain: true`,
HotLoop publishes that component's commands retained, and says so everywhere a
person decides about it: the Discovered screen flags it and the tag editor
says it in plain words. Understand what that means before you arm one: the
broker keeps the last command and hands it to the device every time the device
reconnects, at three in the morning, with nobody's hand on anything. The
command still went through the gate and is still on the audit trail with a name
against it; it just happens again.

There is no "publish this to that topic" anywhere: not in automations, not in
scripts, not in MCP. That would be a side door round the gate with a nicer name.
In the code, two things in discovery publish: the driver's write, which only the
gate reaches, and the birth. A guard test type-checks the driver package and
fails the build if anything else calls either, with a planted bypass to prove
it bites.

## Templates

No Python, no Jinja engine. `internal/mqtttpl` is a hand-written subset of Jinja
sized to what publishers actually send: lookups, a conditional, a dict used as a
lookup table, a few filters. No loops, so a template costs what its length
costs.

`{% set name = value %}` is in, and only that shape: Zigbee2MQTT writes every
thermostat's mode as `{% set values = {'manual':'heat', ...} %}` and then looks
it up, and a thermostat whose mode can't be read is a thermostat you can't
trust. No namespace, no unpacking, no block form. `.keys()` is in too, only as
the right side of `in`, because that's the one place those templates use it.

| <span class="sr-only">Details</span> | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|
| Structure | text, `{{ expr }}`, `{% if %}` / `{% elif %}` / `{% else %}`, `{% set name = value %}`, `{# comments #}`, `-` whitespace control |
| Variables | value templates: `value`, `value_json` (only when the payload is JSON), `entity_id`, `name`; command templates: `value`, `entity_id`, `name` |
| Expressions | literals, `.attr`, `['key']`, `[0]`, slices, `+ - * / // % **`, `~`, comparisons, `and or not`, `in`, `x if c else y`, `.get(key, default)` on a mapping, `in mapping.keys()` |
| Tests | `defined`, `undefined`, `none`, `number`, `integer`, `float`, `boolean`, `string`, `mapping`, `sequence`, `true`, `false`, `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, `in`, `odd`, `even`, `divisibleby` |
| Filters | `float`, `int`, `round`, `bool`, `default`/`d`, `string`, `lower`, `upper`, `capitalize`, `title`, `trim`, `replace`, `truncate`, `abs`, `length`/`count`, `min`, `max`, `tojson`, `to_json`, `from_json`, `is_defined`, `iif` |
| Functions | `float()`, `int()`, `bool()`, `iif()`, `min()`, `max()` |

Where the format documents a filter differently from stock Jinja, HotLoop
follows the format. The one that matters: **`float` and `int` without a default
fail** on something that isn't a number. Stock Jinja quietly hands back `0`, and
that's the zero that says the tank is empty when the sensor stopped answering.

Values render the way Python's `str()` renders them, because that's what every
publisher's configs were written against: `True`, `None`, `21.0` stays `21.0`.
It isn't cosmetic. Zigbee2MQTT's contact sensor announces `payload_on: false`
and matches the rendered `False`.

**A missing key is an error unless you handled it.** `{{ value_json.temperature }}`
on a payload without one is a bad reading saying so, not an empty string.
`default`, `is defined` and a bare `{% if value_json.x %}` handle it on purpose,
and are fine.

**Outside the subset, refused when the config arrives**, with where: "value
template not supported: filter `regex_findall_index` is not supported at column
12". The component is still made, so you can see it exists, and it reads bad
with that reason. There's no best-effort partial render and no "use the raw
payload instead". Two real templates are refused on purpose: `now()` (a value
that depends on when HotLoop evaluated it isn't a reading of the device), and a
Zigbee2MQTT event template that builds regex patterns with namespaces and
`regex_findall`.

Limits: 4 KiB of template, nesting 32 deep, 64 KiB of output, 64-bit integers
(an overflow is an error, not a wrap).

How it's checked: Pallets Jinja2 3.1.6 runs in a throwaway container in CI, and
every case in the oracle battery (grammar, operators, truthiness, whitespace
control, `str()` rendering) has to come out the same as it does there. The
format's own filters, which aren't stock Jinja, have hand-written cases citing
the documented behavior each one holds us to. Every template in the
recordings has to parse. The parser and the evaluator are fuzzed.

## What HotLoop builds from what

| Component | Tag | Entities |
|---|---|---|
| `sensor` | `float` when it has a unit, a state class or a numeric device class, else `string` | sensor |
| `binary_sensor` | `bool` | binary_sensor |
| `switch` | `bool` | binary_sensor, and a switch control entity, unarmed |
| `number` | `float`, with the config's `min`/`max` as the tag's range | sensor, and a number control entity, unarmed, with min, max and step |
| `text` | `string` | sensor, and a text control entity, unarmed |
| `select` | `string`, reading only one of its options | sensor, and a select with the config's options, unarmed |
| `button` | `string`, taking a press and reading nothing | a single-shot button, unarmed (the tag's own read entity is made hidden) |
| `light` | `bool` on/off; `float` brightness 0 to 100 % when it has one | a light, unarmed |
| `cover` | `string` state, which also takes `open`, `close` and `stop`; `float` position 0 to 100 % when it has one | a cover, unarmed |
| `valve` | `string` state; `float` position 0 to 100 % if it reports one; `bool` command (open or close) and `bool` stop, commanded and never read | a valve, unarmed, its stop single shot |
| `event` | `string`, the event type | an event |
| `device_automation` (a trigger) | `string`, `<type>_<subtype>` when its payload arrives | an event, one per trigger |
| `lock` | `string`, read in its own words and taking `lock`, `unlock`, `open` | a lock, unarmed |
| `fan` | `bool` on/off; `float` speed 0 to 100 %; `string` preset and direction; `bool` oscillation, each when it has one | a fan, unarmed |
| `siren` | `bool` | a siren, unarmed |
| `scene` | `bool`, a press | a single-shot button, unarmed |
| `notify` | `string`, a message, commanded and never read | a notifier, unarmed |
| `update` | `string` installed and latest versions | an update: on when they differ. Its install command is never sent |
| `device_tracker` | `string`, `home`, `not_home` or a zone | a tracker |
| `tag` | `string`, the tag's id when one is scanned | an event |
| `climate` | `string` mode; `float` setpoint, low and high setpoints and humidity setpoint, each with the config's `min_temp`/`max_temp` (or `min_humidity`/`max_humidity`) as its range; `float` room temperature and humidity; `string` fan, swing and preset modes and action; `bool` power, commanded and never read; each when it has one | a thermostat, unarmed |
| `humidifier` | `bool` on/off; `float` humidity setpoint in its range; `string` mode and action; `float` room humidity | a humidifier, unarmed |
| `water_heater` | `string` mode; `float` setpoint in its range and current temperature; `bool` power, commanded and never read | a water heater, unarmed |
| `alarm_control_panel` | `string` state, read in the format's words and taking the actions its `supported_features` list, each its own payload | an alarm panel, unarmed |
| `vacuum` | `string` state, taking the actions its `supported_features` list; `float` battery; `string` fan speed, each from its JSON state | a vacuum, unarmed |
| `lawn_mower` | `string` activity; `bool` start mowing, pause and dock, each a press on its own topic, commanded and never read | a mower, unarmed |
| `camera` | `string`, a short hash of the latest picture; the picture itself is held in memory | a camera |
| `image` | the same, for a picture on `image_topic`; or `string`, the URL from `url_topic` | an image |

For a light, a cover, a valve, an event, a trigger and every component in the
rows after them, the tags' own read entities are made hidden: the thing is
one entity on the screens. Each tag
still gets armed on its own, so a cover whose position you trust and whose
open and close you don't can be exactly that. A thing that gains a value after
it was accepted (a firmware that starts reporting a brightness) is a change
for review, and when a person applies it the entity gets the role along with
the tag.

A JSON-schema light's state messages are folded together, because the schema
sends what changed: a message with only a brightness, or Zigbee2MQTT's
`last_seen` alone, leaves the light on. Its color, color temperature and
effect are shown as attributes, not commanded; on, off and brightness are,
and the Discovered screen says so for a light that has color. A default-schema
light's color topics are the same: not read, not commanded, and listed. The
template schema isn't supported and says so. Cover tilt isn't read or
commanded, and says so.

A device trigger fires only on its own `payload`: Zigbee2MQTT puts every
action of a button on one topic, and each trigger is one of them. A trigger
with no `payload` fires on anything on its topic.

A fan's speed reads on the config's own `speed_range_min`..`speed_range_max`
the way the format does: the first step above off is the first percent. A
level the config says can't happen (an ESPHome fan announcing four steps and
reporting 25) is a bad reading saying so, not 625 percent.

The Discovered screen lists every topic a component's commands can go to: a
light's brightness topic, a fan's speed topic, as well as the main one, and
flags each that's outside what the component reads, inside the prefix, or
claimed by another device.

A thermostat's or a water heater's setpoint range is the config's own, and the
format's default when it gives none (7 to 35 °C for a thermostat, 43.3 to 60 °C
for a water heater, in °F when the config says `temperature_unit: F`). It's the
tag's range, so the gate refuses 31 °C to a radiator valve that tops out at 30
before anything is sent. Its modes are the config's list, and a mode it doesn't
list is refused the same way. The screens offer exactly those, and when an
applied change brings a new mode, the screens get it too.

An alarm panel's `code` is what a consumer's screen asks for before it sends
anything. In HotLoop, who may arm or disarm is the gate's call, with the tag
armed by a person and every command audited, so the action goes out as the
config says. A panel whose command template wants the code itself (`{{ code }}`)
can't be commanded: HotLoop has no code to put there, and the Discovered
screen says so. A vacuum's `send_command_topic` isn't used: an arbitrary command is
exactly what HotLoop can't check against the config.

A camera's or an image's picture is held in memory, the latest one per
component, up to 4 MiB, and served by `GET /api/entities/{entity_id}/image`.
HotLoop keeps it only if the bytes are a JPEG, PNG, GIF or WebP, whatever the
config's `content_type` claims: an SVG is a document that runs script, and a
"picture" that runs script on whoever opens the dashboard is a hole. Its tag
holds a short hash, so the history says when the picture changed without a
database full of JPEGs. An image announced by URL is a link: HotLoop shows it,
only if it's http or https, and never fetches it, because a server that
fetches whatever address a device names can be pointed at anything on the
network. Neither is logged in the logbook; a camera changes every second and
tag_history already has every change.

Every component the format defines becomes something. A component it doesn't
define (a `kettle`) is stored with what it announced and listed as making
nothing. The format has no date, time or datetime component, so neither does
this list.

Entity IDs are HotLoop's, made from the device and the tag. A config's
`object_id` and `default_entity_id` are ignored: a config doesn't get to pick a
name in HotLoop's namespace, and a hostile one would pick `switch.boiler_main`.

## Untrusted, all of it

Everything a config says came from whoever can publish on the prefix. So:

- names and text are capped and stripped of control characters, and the screen
  puts them on the page as text, never HTML;
- a topic with a wildcard, a `$` topic, or a `~` with no base to put there is
  refused with the reason;
- a config over 64 KiB is refused; a device can't have more than 512
  components; no more than 256 devices can wait for a decision on one broker;
  config messages past 200 a second are dropped and counted. Every refusal is
  counted and shown on the Discovered screen, never dropped without a word;
- HotLoop subscribes to `<prefix>/+/+/config` and `<prefix>/+/+/+/config`,
  never `#` under the prefix, so a stray deep topic can't make it parse anything;
- a state payload over 256 KiB, or one that isn't UTF-8, is a bad reading.

With anonymous connections allowed on the embedded broker, anyone on the network
can announce devices and publish to any command topic, and the Discovered
screen says so in red. Give each device its own login made in HotLoop, from
its profile, named after its topic ([BROKER.md](/iot/broker/)): then it can
announce itself and nothing else, and it can't touch another device's command
topic.

## The broker side

Discovery runs on the embedded broker (see [BROKER.md](/iot/broker/)), on by
default whenever the broker is. HotLoop's own client logs in with a login made
at every start and held only in memory: there's nothing to configure and
nothing in a backup to leak. It publishes one thing of its own, the birth
(`<prefix>/status` = `online`), which makes publishers that listen for it
announce again.

| Variable | Default | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_DISCOVERY` | `true` | Listen for announcements on the embedded broker |
| `HOTLOOP_BROKER_DISCOVERY_PREFIX` | `homeassistant` | The topic prefix they arrive under |

One client per broker, `hotloop-disc-embedded`, shared by the listener and every
discovered device's driver. An `--mcp-stdio` helper opens none: a second client
with the same id would kick the Gateway's off the broker every few seconds. With
several replicas on one database, only the one holding the discovery lock
listens.

## Other brokers

Plenty of plants already run a broker: a Mosquitto that's the UNS, the one a
Zigbee2MQTT box brought with it. HotLoop listens to those too. Settings, MQTT,
add a broker: an id (it names the broker in every device that came from it),
where it is, a login, and the prefix its publishers announce under. The broker
doesn't have to be on, and HotLoop doesn't need the embedded one to do this.

Three things are different from HotLoop's own broker, on purpose:

- **Devices wait in the inbox.** On a busy plant broker, "show up on their
  own" means three hundred devices on the screen before lunch. So an announced
  device is listed on the Discovered screen, nothing made and nothing reading,
  until somebody accepts it. Then it's made, it reads, and its points can be
  armed like any other. A broker you trust to dump everything on you can be
  switched to "devices appear on their own".
- **No last will.** HotLoop connects without one. An `offline` will on a
  shared broker would tell every other publisher on it that something went
  away, when it was only HotLoop. The tests check the CONNECT packet itself,
  and pull the plug on the connection to prove nothing gets said.
- **Its ACLs are its own.** HotLoop can't see who published what on somebody
  else's broker, so there's no "announced by login" there, and what each login
  may touch is that broker's business. Give HotLoop a login that reads the
  prefix and the topics of the devices you accept, and writes the birth and
  the command topics, nothing else. For Mosquitto:

  ```
  user hotloop
  topic read homeassistant/+/+/config
  topic read homeassistant/+/+/+/config
  topic write homeassistant/status
  # the devices you accept, for example a Zigbee2MQTT bridge:
  topic read zigbee2mqtt/#
  topic write zigbee2mqtt/+/set
  ```

**Listen-only** is for a broker HotLoop must not speak on: the production UNS,
somebody else's plant. HotLoop never publishes anything there. No birth, no
command. That's the session's rule, not the screen's: its publish refuses, and
the write gate refuses every command to its devices with "the broker
plant-uns is listen-only", dry run included, even on a device somebody accepted and a point
somebody armed. Its login needs nothing but `topic read` lines.

The password is sealed with the device credential key
(`HOTLOOP_SECRET_KEY_FILE`), like a UniFi console's, and never comes back out
of the API. Without a key a broker with a password is refused, not stored in
the clear. A backup carries it sealed and restores under the same rule as a
device's credentials ([BACKUP.md](/iot/backup/)). A broker whose password can't be
opened is listed, not connected, and says why.

Change a broker and the listener and every device from it connect again with
the new settings. Switch one off and its devices stay, reading bad and saying
their broker isn't running here. Removing one takes the inbox with it, and is
refused, naming them, while devices somebody accepted from it still exist.

## On an Edge Relay

An Edge Relay discovers too, with the same code, but it has no database to keep
a decision in and no screen to make one on. So it takes whatever it hears,
reads it and forwards it over Sparkplug, and nothing it finds can be armed: its
tags are read-only like every discovered tag, its devices are never accepted,
and the relay has no write path at all. Name the brokers in its device file; see
[EDGE-RELAY.md](/edge-relay/reference/). A device you can command gets
there the other way: accepted and armed on a Gateway, in a file it pushes. It
forgets what it heard when it stops, and hears it again from the broker.

## Restarts and replays

Accepted devices run from their device rows. HotLoop doesn't need a single
retained message to come back up with its plant.

The embedded broker keeps nothing across a restart, so every config is "missing"
afterwards. **A missing config is not a withdrawal**: only an explicit empty one
is. Anything else would withdraw the whole plant every time the box reboots.
Until a device sends its next state, its entities read unknown, never the value
from before the restart dressed up as current.

A broker that replays hundreds of retained configs at once is one batch: two
seconds of quiet, one pass, one reload. A replay of what's already on record
changes nothing and reloads nothing.

## Backups

`mqtt_devices` (who accepted and ignored what), `mqtt_configs` (every config as
it arrived, byte for byte) and `mqtt_discovered` (each component, normalised)
are in every backup. The decisions are the part no device can announce back.

## The API

Under `/api/discovery`. See [API.md](/iot/api/#mqtt-discovery).

## Found on the network

The same screen lists devices HotLoop heard on the plant network over mDNS,
SSDP and DHCP, decided about the same way. See
[NETWORK-DISCOVERY.md](/iot/network-discovery/).
